body.heading: The first minute belongs to whoever claims it
paragraphs: For most people, the day begins with an ambush: the alarm, the phone, the news, the list. Within two minutes of waking, the mind is fully employed by other people’s priorities, and the tone — slightly rushed, slightly braced — can persist for hours.
One deliberate breath, taken before any of that, is a tiny act of repossession. It says: the day will make its requests soon enough, but its first moment is mine.

body.heading: How one breath becomes a ritual
paragraphs: Sit up, or stay lying down, and take one slow breath — in through the nose, out through the mouth, longer out than in. Feel it completely: the cool air arriving, the chest rising, the long soft exit. One breath, done with your whole attention, takes about ten seconds.

Attach it to the alarm so it cannot be forgotten: alarm, sit up, one breath, then the day. If you like, pair it with a single sentence — “Today, gently” or “One thing at a time” — not as a spell, but as a heading for the day’s page.

body.heading: Small beginnings compound
paragraphs: One breath will not transform a morning, and it is not meant to. Its power is in its reliability: it happens every day, it cannot fail, and it marks a border between sleeping and striving that most of us otherwise cross unconsciously.

Some people find the breath grows — two breaths, a minute sitting on the bed’s edge, a stretch. Let it grow if it wants to. The seed of every durable morning practice is a beginning so small it survives the worst morning of the year.

takeaway: Alarm, sit up, one full breath: claim the first moment before the day claims you.
